direct_claims: This chart is a scatter plot comparing 'Learning-adjusted years of schooling' against the 'Electoral Democracy Index' for various countries in the year 2020.
It was produced by the publication Our World in Data.
The data sources used are the World Bank, based on the methodology of Filmer et al. (2018), and the V-Dem Institute.

Learning-adjusted years of schooling combines the quantity of schooling with the quality of learning, accounting for the fact that a year of school in one country may not yield the same learning outcomes as in another.
The 'Electoral Democracy Index' is a standard political science metric from V-Dem that ranges from 0 (least democratic) to 1 (most democratic).
derived_claims: The purpose of the chart is to visualize the relationship between a nation's educational outcomes and its level of democratic governance across different global regions.

High educational outcomes (above 10 LAYS) are achieved by both highly democratic nations like Poland, Slovenia, and Australia and highly non-democratic or semi-democratic nations like Singapore and Hong Kong.
The presence of highly educated, non-democratic nations like Singapore and China shows that authoritarian regimes can successfully build high-performing education systems.
Democratic nations like Liberia and Senegal have low learning-adjusted years of schooling.
European nations (blue-grey) are heavily clustered in the upper-right quadrant, indicating high education and high democracy.
African nations (purple) are predominantly located in the lower half of the chart, representing lower learning-adjusted years of schooling across a wide range of democracy scores.
speculative_claims: Democratic governance is not a strict prerequisite for high-quality education systems.
It challenges classical modernization theory, which suggests that rising education levels inevitably lead to democratic transitions.
Democratic transitions do not automatically guarantee high-quality public services or educational infrastructure.
